0.0.n: A standard evening greeting; the final は is pronounced わ.

1.0.n: Sets the time for the speaker’s introduction.

1.1.n: Marks 今日 as the topic: the speaker is introducing what they will have today.

1.2.n: The first part of the convenience store name セブン-イレブン.

1.4.n: The second part of the convenience store name セブン-イレブン.

1.5.n: Marks 7-Eleven as the place where the product was released.

2.0.n: Combines with 月 to make 2月, February.

2.1.n: After a number, 月 names a calendar month; 2月 is February.

2.2.n: Read とおか, the special reading for the tenth day of a month.

2.3.n: Marks the specific date of the product’s release.

2.4.n: Past passive form of 発売する; it describes 新商品 as something that was put on sale.

2.5.n: The phrase before it tells you when this item went on sale.

3.0.n: A polite way to refer to the item the speaker is presenting.

3.1.n: Shows that こちら is the object of いただきます.

3.2.n: Polite humble form of 食べる here; also commonly said before starting a meal.

4.0.n: A product name combining チョコ, ブラウニー, and サンド, a shortened form of sandwich.

4.2.n: Part of the product name; パキ suggests a crisp snapping texture, and チョコ is short for chocolate.

5.0.n: Short for 税込み, indicating that the stated price already includes tax.

5.1.n: 円 follows the number to give the price in Japanese currency.

0.tip: The は in こんばんは is pronounced わ, not は.

1.tip: This line continues into the next: で connects the store to the product’s release.

2.tip: Japanese puts the description was released on February 10th before the noun new product.

3.lit: This one, I will humbly eat.
3.tip: いただきます politely announces that the speaker will eat the item.

4.tip: サンド is a common shortened form of サンドイッチ in Japanese food names.

5.tip: 税込 means you do not need to add tax to the displayed price.
